data.title: Rastislav's ancient Devín and the record of it from 871
data.excerpt: Mgr. Peter Baláž examines the nameless Great Moravian sites described in the Annals of Fulda – the “very strong rampart” of 855, the “ineffable fortress unlike all the most ancient ones” of 869 and the “urbs antiqua Rastizi” of 871. He argues that urbs need not mean a capital, that the ancient hillfort and the one unlike all ancient ones cannot be the same place, and that the hillfort at the confluence of the Morava and the Danube best fits the record of 871.

data.metaDescription: Peter Baláž on locating the nameless Great Moravian hillforts of the Annals of Fulda and on Rastislav's ancient Devín, the Dowina of August 864.

children.text: We bring you a very interesting article contributing to the debate on the localisation of the Great Moravian hillforts written about in the Annals of Fulda, which scholars have so far (apart from Dowina-Devín) failed to identify convincingly with specific hillforts known today. The author of the article is Mgr. Peter Baláž and it was originally published in Historický zborník no. 1/2013 under the title: K starobylosti a jedinečnosti „urbs antiqua Rastizi“ (On the antiquity and uniqueness of the “urbs antiqua Rastizi”). It was reviewed by doc. Michal Slivka. We publish it with the author's permission.
Rastislav's ancient Devín and the record of it from 871.

The place at the confluence of the Morava and the Danube is linked, in August 864, with the only written mention in the whole of the Annals of Fulda that gives the proper name of a Great Moravian site. It testifies that it was here, “in a certain hillfort which in the language of that people is called Dowina”, that Prince Rastislav was besieged by the army of Louis the German. The prince of Great Moravia resisted the East Frankish ruler here for some time, but the latter finally broke his resistance and Rastislav swore loyalty to him. Yet this conclusion of peace was in the end beneficial for Rastislav in both the political and the ecclesiastical sphere. Several written mentions from the second half of the 9th century also belong to the territory of Great Moravia and refer to sites that are not given a proper name, only a description of them being recorded. Here we shall focus on the three most important ones recorded in the Annals of Fulda. The first of these mentions is the one linked to the events of 855, when Rastislav was protected against the East Frankish king Louis the German by a “very strong rampart”. The second mention relates to the year 869, when Louis's son Charles came at the head of an army “to that ineffable fortress of Rastislav, unlike all the most ancient ones” and, “relying on God's help, destroyed by fire the surrounding fortifications in that territory”. The third is connected with the year 871. At that time Svatopluk “entered the old hillfort of Rastislav”. This happened when Prince Rastislav was already in Bavarian captivity and the Moravian part of Great Moravia was occupied by Frankish military units. In the Nitra region, which had retained its independent position, resistance arose under the leadership of Svatopluk's successor Slavomír against the Moravian margraves Wilhelm and Engelschalk and the Frankish garrisons in Moravia. Thanks to this resistance the newly captured Svatopluk was released by Carloman. At the head of a Frankish expedition he came to one of the Moravian hillforts, the one that was the “urbs antiqua”, and which the Franks also knew in connection with Rastislav. Immediately afterwards, however, Svatopluk went over to Slavomír's side and defeated the Frankish army he had brought with him.

children.text: The term
“urbs”
in the relevant part of the Annals of Fulda did not denote the central or capital city of the country and could probably have been identical with the term
“civitas”
. Equating the term
“urbs”
with the central site of Great Moravia has no justification in the case of the relevant Mainz chronicler of the Annals of Fulda.
The meaning of the second descriptive word
“antiqua”
is most probably “ancient”.

This need not, however, have been merely a one-off designation by a person who noticed the antiquity of this site, but also a kind of provisional naming of the site or sites (“that ineffable fortress”), used for a time by foreigners until they had adopted its proper name.

The problem with the whole perspective on the “Devín – Velehrad” question, or rather Devín and the two central Moravian hillforts of Mikulčice and Uherské Hradiště, is that it and all the related partial questions are inappropriately subsumed under the question of the capital of Great Moravia.
The very important descriptive designations of the two Moravian sites of 869 and 871 have thus been assessed incompletely in the analysis of their localisation.
In the analysis of the localisation of
“urbs antiqua Rastizi
” the term
“urbs”
is thus mistakenly expected to inform us of this status as a capital. And the term
“antiqua”
refers us, according to these views, to the ancient but purely Slavic beginnings of this hillfort.
V. Brandl was already unsure of his own argument in favour of
“urbs”
as the capital of Great Moravia: “further, the word
urbs

seems to me worth noting here (although I do not attach great weight to this argument), which, standing on its own, means a capital city at least in classical Latin; medieval writers, although here and there they preserve this distinction between civitas
= town and urbs
= capital city, nevertheless do not follow it everywhere and always”.
Later, however, the connection between “
urbs”
and the capital of Great Moravia becomes clearer for some. J. Zavadil does state that “the annalist, after all, also designates Ratisbona (Regensburg) once as
urbs
, and another time as
civitas
”. But this does not prevent him from seeing the designation
“urbs”,
to which the annalist attached
“Rastizi”
as that “from which it emerges most clearly that by it he wished to single out Rostislav's principal seat”.
L. Bílková, Z. Fiala and M. Karbulová, although they state that “not even the use of the term
urbs
explains much”, finally come to the conclusion that as
“urbs”
“it is rather a centre that is designated, as was also suggested by the situation in Great Moravia, where the seat of the rulers was designated in this way”.
M. Bláhová states that in the Annals of Fulda, in the case of the terms “
civitas”
and “
urbs”
“there is probably no fundamental difference in the meaning and use of the two terms”.
But for Slavic sites, out of the two terms given in the whole of the Annals of Fulda,
“urbs antiqua Rastizi
” (which she already translates directly as “Rastislav's seat”!) and Mosaburg, she concludes that “the expression
urbs
rather denotes tribal centres or rulers' seats”.
The authors of Magnae Moraviae fontes historici I refer to a preference for the designation
“urbs”
for a capital city, the example of which is supposed to be Regensburg.
M. Bláhová, by contrast, states: “the contribution of several authors must again be taken into account when assessing the terminology of the Annals of Fulda”.
Likewise, in her analysis of the Annals of Fulda and of the terms
“urbs”
and
“civitas”
she states that “their use is to a considerable extent influenced by the preferences of the individual authors”.
In 1973 D. Třeštík makes a simple statement about
“urbs”
in the relevant Mainz chronicler of the
Annals of Fulda on the basis of P. Ratkoš's analysis: “the use of the term
urbs,
which the annalist otherwise applies only to the most important cities in the East Frankish and West Frankish empires and in Italy, is striking here”.
In his contribution P. Ratkoš states of
“urbs”
“the meaning is the same as in the case of
civitas”.
D. Třeštík returns to this view of his several times later and builds on it his argument in favour of
“urbs”
as the capital of Great Moravia.

Of the hillforts in central Moravia, at least one for certain – the one that was “unlike all the most ancient ones” – could not be compared by the chronicler with any one of the many sites known to him. This further nameless site of 869, known in connection with Rastislav as the “ineffable fortress/hillfort (
ineffabilis munitio)
was “(that)
illa”
, that is, generally known.
It had no link, however, to any other site known to the chronicler, and so for him it had no known past either, because it was “unlike all” sites, even the “most ancient ones”.

There are several views that conflate the descriptions of the two Great Moravian sites of 869 and 871. According to F. Palacký, in 869 “Charles got as far as Welehrad, Rostislav's principal seat, whose enclosures were for that age extraordinary and unexampled...”
by which he means
“old Welehrad”
, today's Uherské Hradiště.
According to him, in 871 too Svatopluk came with Carloman's army “right up to Welehrad” and “himself entered the city”.
Václav Novotný wrongly assigns the attributes of Rastislav's hillfort of 869 to
“urbs antiqua Rastizi”
, which he sees as “that wonderfully fortified, great stronghold of Rastislav”, and it was “to that fearsome stronghold” that the Bavarian army led by Svatopluk came.
According to I. L. Červinka, Slavomír's power also included “that wonderfully fortified great hillfort of Rostislav (Děvín)”.
Similarly, M. Kučera writes of how in 871 Svatopluk “turned up with the Bavarian army beneath the walls of Rastislav's mighty and (as the chronicler notes) unprecedented stronghold”.
But a site that for the chronicler is “old
(antiqua)
” cannot be assigned to the hillfort “unlike all the most ancient ones
(omnibus antiquissimis dissimilem)
”. These designations stand in natural opposition to each other.

If one of the pair of hillforts, Mikulčice or Uherské Hradiště, were not the “ineffable fortress of Rastislav”, what other descriptive name should belong to it? And what descriptive name could Devín have had among the Bavarians? The reason for the perception of the antiquity of
“urbs Rastizi”
is supposed to be the very position and character of the hillfort.

If a site had certain distinctive and visible features, it was perceived through them also in relation to the past. Mikulčice, Uherské Hradiště or another site in central Moravia offer no sufficient arguments for antiquity in the 9th century. Slavic beginnings, a palisade wall or a position on the Amber Road provide no justification for the East Frankish designation of this site on the middle course of the river Morava as
“antiqua”.
Devín, as a dominant rocky eminence with a strategic position

in the lifetime of a direct participant in the events, situated on the border between the Eastern March and Moravia, which was then formed by the river Danube, and earlier the frontier between the classical and the barbarian world,

has weightier grounds for antiquity. In this connection, those who in the Early Middle Ages observed this hillfort and its surroundings were very probably aware of its occupation and use in earlier periods. In the matter of antiquity, Great Moravian Devín clearly differs from the hillforts further north on the river Morava, or in the Dyje region.
The importance of the designation and perception of the site
“urbs Rastizi”

as ancient was realised towards the end of his life by the Czech archaeologist and historian Josef Poulík as well. He sees no contradiction, however, between the descriptions of the sites of 869 and 871, and places both at Mikulčice. This
“urbs antiqua Rastizi”
presupposes, in his view, a “new city”, and this “new city” is supposed to be the enclosures of Staré Město – Uherské Hradiště, a few kilometres away.
In 1961 the archaeologist J. Dekan published a short summary of archaeological and historical research concerning Devín in the magazine Príroda a spoločnosť.
On this “truly broad historical and archaeological basis of knowledge” he proceeds “to the final solution of the Devín question”.

He refutes the views of some Czech historians that Devín was the centre of Great Moravia and the seat of Rastislav, and identifies this hillfort with the entry of the Annals of Fulda for 864. He locates the “ineffable fortress of Rastislav” and the “old city of Rastislav” in the Moravian interior, from where the important early medieval discoveries appear to him in a “captivatingly magnificent light”.

Archaeological excavation at Devín has continued after J. Dekan, more than half a century on. Thanks to continuing archaeological research, the perception of Devín is no longer entirely of the same dimension as in his day, but has again moved on.

Yet J. Dekan's conclusions and certainty are still taken at face value in approaching this question, and are set against the idiosyncratic views of some Czech historians and archaeologists of the first half of the 20th century, who united all the descriptive written mentions of the Annals of Fulda and the capital of Great Moravia in Great Moravian Devín.

This question, however, needs to be viewed separately, in an individual approach to each mention of Great Moravian sites in the Annals of Fulda. Alongside the demolition of the myths of L. Červinka, E. Šimek, Ľ. Zachar, I. L. Zavadil, and at present E. Šubjaková, who celebrate Devín as the principal seat of Svatopluk or Rastislav,

it is necessary to continue with a thorough analysis of the description and localisation of the “old city of Rastislav” and likewise with an analysis of the description of the “ineffable fortress of Rastislav”.

In the course of more than 150 years of effort, often tendentious, attempts to solve the problem of the nameless Great Moravian sites have frequently ended in blind alleys. Lumír Poláček states that the attempts to identify
“urbs antiqua Rastizi”
and
“ineffabilis Rastizi munitio”
with Mikulčice or with Staré Město – Uherské Hradiště are not successful.
A critical analysis of the term “
urbs”

, which the annalist in question does not reserve, in the case of Slavic hillforts, for the most important Moravian site, together with an understanding of the whole descriptive designation, reveal the reason for this failure in the case of
“urbs antiqua Rastizi”

. The “ancient” hillfort of 871 and the hillfort of 869 that was “unlike all the most ancient ones” naturally stand in mutually contradictory positions. It is impossible to connect them. The attribute of the one site was “antiquity”, while the attribute of the other was “dissimilarity to antiquity”, which consisted in the fact that the site could not be compared with, or assigned to, any sites known to the chronicler or his informant, not even the most ancient ones.
Vincent Brandl objects to the connection of Devín with
“urbs antiqua Rastizi”

: “In the first place we have reason to think so because the chronicler does not give the name Dovina, which he would probably not have omitted... he would have added even now ‘in urbem antiquam Rastizi Dovinam ingressus est’; but since he did not supply it, it seems that he wished to indicate another town, or stronghold”.

But did the chronicler know that it really was Devín that was involved in 871? Would a participant in the Frankish expedition led by Svatopluk have known that this expedition came to Devín, whose name some of the participants in the campaign of seven years earlier had already learned? Did those who saved their lives before Svatopluk's massacre by prudently leaving the camp, and who gave the chronicler an account of it, know the oikonym of this site? If so, V. Brandl's view would be decisive. But does such a simple rule apply here, that from the first written mention with a real name no descriptive designation can ever again refer to it? A participant in the expedition of 871 need not have been on the campaign of 864, nor need the information about the proper name of the site have reached him in any other way. He may therefore not have known the proper name of this hillfort when he gave his account of the event that took place in 871 in Great Moravia. Although some of the inhabitants of the East Frankish Empire already knew this site, we cannot strictly expect the chronicler's informant, or the chronicler himself, to have known this piece of information, that it was the same site. Frankish military expeditions were not a geographical or topographical mapping of enemy country. It was not the chronicler's main concern to inform the court circles of the East Frankish Empire about the hillforts of Great Moravia and to collect information about further sites in this territory. The problem the chroniclers had was rather how to describe a past event in a politically acceptable way. And the tendentiousness of the chroniclers of the Annals of Fulda is well known.

We would evidently be asking of the informants and recorders of the reports in the Annals of Fulda something that lay entirely outside their purpose: to give precise data about Moravian sites. That was not the object of their interest. Neither the East Frankish king nor one of his sons set out to capture and subdue some Great Moravian hillfort on the basis of the precise topographical localisation of the Annals of Fulda.

The informant described the deed to the chronicler, not topographical details. P. Ratkoš points out that, as regards settlement terminology, the Annals of Fulda have a poorer range of terms for the territory of Great Moravia, since the chronicler drew his information second-hand and his geographical knowledge of Great Moravia was probably inaccurate.
Rastislav's
“ineffabilis munitio”
was
“illa

”, that is, generally known. If it was the description of the site and not its proper name that entered the awareness of the inhabitants of the East Frankish Empire, this description could have coexisted there for some time even after the proper name became known, and that without both necessarily being known at once. This was a gradual process of adopting the proper name of a site in a distant country. Dowina is still called thus “in the language of that people”,

that is, this is the first encounter with the proper name of this site, which is still foreign to the people of the informant and the chronicler. The genitive form of the name “(from) Devín” also speaks for this.

Brandl's view can, however, also be turned round. If the Moravian sites of 864 and 871 were to be the same, why is it not stated that in 864 Louis “besieged Rastislav in a certain ancient stronghold which in the language of that people is called Dowina”? If the sites of 869 and 871 were to be the same, why did the chronicler not write in 869: “Charles came to that ineffable, extensive, ancient hillfort of Rastislav, unlike all the most ancient ones”? Or if the sites of 855 and 871 were the same, why is it not stated in 855 “protected, it is said, by a very strong and ancient rampart”? Or likewise, if the sites of 855 and 869 were the same, why is it not stated, for example, “protected, it is said, by a very strong rampart which is unlike all the most ancient ones”? Despite the fact that the individual mentions do not in reality read in this way, the identity of the last-named sites, those of 855 and 869, is possible.
It is therefore evident that one cannot proceed in this way.
Nor did the historians of the following generations build on V. Brandl's argument. They argued for the incompatibility of Devín with
“ineffabilis munitio”
and
“urbs antiqua”
in a different way. Of these arguments the greatest weight attaches to the term
“illa”
of 869, which refers to a generally known site.
However,
“urbs antiqua Rastizi”
was not this
“illa”

. To base a solution on the idea that from August 864 all those who came to Great Moravia from the East Frankish Empire knew the proper name of Devín is therefore highly problematic. The first written mention with the real name of a site cannot be taken as binding for general knowledge of that proper name in the period after this first mention, in all subsequent written records concerning the site in question. Everything depended on what topographical information was obtained by the participant in a given expedition who then gave his report to the chronicler. As an example we have already noted that in 864 the name Dowina had not even been properly adopted by the Bavarians.
The recorder of the Annals of Fulda does not know, in 877, the name of a monastery in Burgundy, although it is known that it bore the name Nantua.
The author of the Altaich continuation of the Annals of Fulda does not know that the pope appointed Wiching bishop of Nitra; for him he is only the “Moravian bishop”,

which is already a broader designation. The entry is from 899, when Nitra had been known to some persons in Bavaria since the time of Archbishop Adalram. The battle between the Old Hungarians and the Bavarians in 907 is placed by the Freising necrologies II and IV, as well as by the Lorsch necrology, merely
“in Oriente”.
They do not know at all that it took place
“ad Brezalauspurc”.

If V. Brandl's argument held, not even a simple independent nameless description could refer to a site that had already been given by its proper name. Brandl's argument, however, ultimately brings us to one fact. If the chronicler, or rather his informant, had known the Slavic name of the hillfort, he would have given it, either on its own or together with the “East Frankish” name. It is evident that if the chronicler's informant uses only the foreigners' descriptive designation, he does not know its Slavic name.
The traditionally interpreted story, in which Svatopluk defeats the Frankish army by Rastislav's seat city and immediately stays on to rule in this hillfort,
is only apparently straightforward and seamless, and it is evident that events took place differently.
“Urbs antiqua Rastizi”

was not the sought-after centre of Great Moravia. Devín at the confluence of the Morava and the Danube never aspired to first place as the capital of Great Moravia, because it was a border stronghold. Its imposing character, however, misled many, and they looked here for a supposed capital. Nor does the mention by the Mainz chronicler of the Annals of Fulda of
“urbs antiqua Rastizi”

bring the information about the centre of the country that some expect. It informs us of the ordinariness and the antiquity of this site in the 9th century, which comes together most probably in the hillfort at the confluence of the Morava and the Danube.
